teaching.task: The cation's known: copper. But copper what? How do you find the anion in a sample, choosing tests that can't fool you, and confirm it?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the cation is only half the salt; eight anion suspects; (2) dilute acid: carbonate takes hydrogen ions and breaks down to CO₂ and water, so it fizzes; CO₂ turns limewater milky as calcium carbonate forms; (3) acetate takes hydrogen ions too, but makes ethanoic acid, not a gas: no fizz, a vinegar smell on warming; neutral FeCl₃ forms a red-brown complex; (4) carbonate also precipitates with barium and silver, so acidify first; HCl would add chloride and H₂SO₄ sulfate; nitric acid is safe because nitrates are all soluble; (5) sulfate: acidified barium, white BaSO₄ that stays in acid (BaCO₃ would dissolve); (6) halides: acidified silver nitrate, white, cream, pale yellow; (7) the colours are close, so ammonia confirms: the less soluble the silver halide, the more ammonia needed to pull silver into a complex: dilute, concentrated, neither; (8) phosphate: yellow Ag₃PO₄, only in neutral solution, because in acid phosphate takes hydrogen ions and stops precipitating; it dissolves in dilute nitric acid, which separates it from AgI; (9) hydroxide: basic to litmus, but carbonate and phosphate are basic too, so test last; hydroxide takes a hydrogen ion from ammonium and releases ammonia, which turns damp red litmus blue; (10) the flowchart; (11) the salt named.
teaching.conversationalApproach: the last video found copper in the prep room bottle, but copper chloride, sulfate and acetate all give the same copper results, so the video asks how to find the anion, choosing tests that cannot fool you, and confirm it. The plan is the same: fresh portions and reagents that react with only a few ions. Dilute acid comes first: carbonate takes hydrogen ions and fizzes carbon dioxide that turns limewater milky, while acetate gives no fizz but a vinegar smell on gentle warming, confirmed by a deep red-brown complex with neutral iron(III) chloride. The surprise is that the acid can create the result: carbonate would fake a positive with barium and silver, so acidify first, but hydrochloric acid would add chloride to the halide test, so use dilute nitric acid there. Acidified barium gives white barium sulfate that stays in acid; acidified silver nitrate gives white, cream and pale yellow silver halides, and ammonia confirms them, since silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia, silver bromide needs concentrated and silver iodide dissolves in neither. Phosphate is tested in a separate neutral portion, because in acid it picks up hydrogen ions and stops precipitating, and its yellow silver phosphate dissolves in dilute nitric acid where silver iodide does not. Hydroxide comes last, because carbonate and phosphate solutions are basic too, and warming with an ammonium salt releases ammonia that turns damp red litmus blue. The full flowchart closes the tests. The memory aid is acid first with an acid that adds none of the ions you are testing for, phosphate in a neutral portion, then white, cream, pale yellow and dilute, concentrated, neither. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback, and the hook bottle is named copper sulfate.
teaching.openingDecision: Back to the prep room. A pale blue precipitate, a deep blue complex and a blue-green flame told us one bottle holds copper ions. But copper what? Copper chloride, copper sulfate and copper acetate all dissolve, and all give the same copper results. The cation's only half the answer. Now we need the anion, and the list has eight: chloride, bromide, iodide, hydroxide, acetate, carbonate, sulfate and phosphate.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) A student acidifies with dilute HCl, then adds AgNO₃, sees a white precipitate and concludes chloride. Explain why invalid, describe the correct test. Tests scene 4's cause. Crossed mistake: "Any acid works: it only removes carbonate." (A2) Separate portions: HNO₃ no effervescence; HNO₃ then Ba(NO₃)₂ no change; HNO₃ then AgNO₃ cream precipitate, dissolves in concentrated but not dilute ammonia. Identify the anion, write the net ionic equation. Tests scenes 2, 5, 6, 7. Crossed mistake: "I⁻: it looked yellowish."
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct qualitative investigations – using flame tests, precipitation and complexation reactions as appropriate – to test for the presence in aqueous solution of the following ions:; cations: barium (Ba2+), calcium (Ca2+), magnesium (Mg2+), lead(II) (Pb2+), silver ion (Ag+), copper(II) (Cu2+), iron(II) (Fe2+), iron(III) (Fe3+); anions: chloride (Cl–), bromide (Br–), iodide (I–), hydroxide (OH–), acetate (CH3COO–), carbonate (CO32–), sulfate (SO42–), phosphate (PO43–)" (The two dashes in the first line are en dashes as printed, not em dashes.) This video covers the eight anions. The cations are chem-m8-c03a; the investigation with unknowns is chem-m8-p03. starts with a sample whose cation is known (copper, from c03a) and stops when the student can choose and order anion tests, explain each reagent choice and interference, identify one unknown anion from observations and write the net ionic equation. It teaches: fresh portions (recall); dilute acid: carbonate fizzes, CO₂ turns limewater milky; acetate gives no fizz but a vinegar smell on warming (ethanoic acid), confirmed by neutral FeCl₃ (red-brown complex); why acidify before barium and silver (carbonate gives white BaCO₃ and pale yellow Ag₂CO₃; acid removes it as CO₂); which acid (HNO₃ for the halide test, because HCl adds chloride; HCl or HNO₃ for sulfate); sulfate: acidified Ba²⁺, white BaSO₄ that stays in acid; halides: acidified AgNO₃, AgCl white, AgBr cream, AgI pale yellow; ammonia confirms (AgCl dissolves in dilute, AgBr in concentrated, AgI in neither); phosphate: AgNO₃ in neutral solution, yellow Ag₃PO₄ that dissolves in dilute HNO₃; why neutral (acid converts phosphate to hydrogen phosphate ions); hydroxide: basic to litmus, but rule out carbonate and phosphate first, then warm with an ammonium salt for NH₃ that turns damp red litmus blue; the full anion flowchart; naming the salt. Not taught: cations (c03a); sulfite, nitrate and other anions; ammonium molybdate for phosphate (author note); the esterification acetate test (site's alternative; author note); procedure and risk table (p03).
